Source commit: b1df327e0319e8c9e9d2d2970a61489595639dce
Dirty local worktree: true These are gauges for human triage, never pass/fail judgements.

Carpet diagnostics

A carpet is a function laid over another to avoid changing it. These numbers flag a module for triage; they never adjudicate one. Do not add a function, module, or folder to bring a number down — that move is the defect being measured.

Method

This report aggregates five tools and performs no analysis of its own, except the shared-name-modifier count, which is marked where it appears. Each section below states which of the five produced its table and with which options.
Tool Version What it contributes
pyan3 2.6.2 name-level uses graph: who calls what
vulture 2.16 dead code, decorator-aware
radon 6.0.1 cyclomatic complexity, maintainability index
grimp 3.15 module import graph
ruff 0.16.2 cross-module private access (SLF001, PLC2701)
Scope: 37 modules across src and tests. Only the roots passed on the command line are scanned — a name whose sole consumer is a different package reads as unreferenced unless that package is a root too. Reproduce the whole report with: 
uv run carpet-scan src --tests tests
Why Check 3 is missing. The section numbers cross-reference the five checks in TODO_additional_code_quality_checks.md, so a finding here can be traced to the rule that motivated it. Four of the five are gauges — measurements with no correct value, read for movement and triage — and they are what this report carries. Check 3 is a gate: an import-linter layers contract asserting the subpackage order someone declared in .importlinter. There is no number to report, only a contract that holds or does not, and wrapping it in a command that always exits 0 would turn a working gate into a line nobody acts on. It runs as a blocking pre-commit hook instead. Its measurable half — whether a folder has become a ladder — is Check 5 below. No timestamp is recorded, deliberately: the report is meant to be diffed between runs.

Public surface with no caller outside its own module

Cross-reference: Check 2. One row per src module with at least 4 public functions. A public function absent from all three buckets has a caller in another module and is genuine public API.
column meaning
module dotted module path, with the common src.<package>. prefix stripped
publics module-level functions not starting with _, as pyan3 saw them
tests only count whose only cross-module callers live in tests
home only count with no cross-module caller that vulture does not call dead
unused count with no cross-module caller that vulture confirms dead
worst cc highest cyclomatic complexity of any block in the file (radon cc)
mi maintainability index for the file, 0-100, higher is better (radon mi)
Generated by: 
pyan3 src tests --root . --uses --no-defines --dot
vulture src tests --min-confidence 60 \
    --ignore-decorators @field_validator,@model_validator,@app.command,@app.default,@property
radon cc src -j
radon mi src -j
Three tools make one row: pyan3 supplies the cross-module edges that fill the buckets, vulture decides whether a name with no external caller is dead or merely used at home, and radon supplies worst cc and mi. The buckets are how the two graphs disagree:
bucket derivation fix
(not listed) pyan3 shows a cross-module edge none — real public API
tests only the only cross-module edges come from tests check the test path
home only no cross-module edge, vulture does not call it dead make private
unused no cross-module edge, vulture confirms it dead delete
Trust the buckets unequally. unused is vulture-confirmed and actionable. home only is unverified: pyan3 documents its own analysis as superficial, with a simplified linear binding model. Three reference forms are known to escape it, and each one inflates home only:
  • a bare name used in a dispatch table in another module
  • a call through a module alias, from pkg import mod then mod.name(...)
  • registration by decorator, e.g. a CLI framework's command decorator
It also over-resolves common names: a project-local normalize, replace or parse can be conflated with str.replace or dataclasses.replace, hiding a real candidate behind a spurious edge. Confirm any home only name by hand before acting on it. (All three forms were verified on the anndata-proteomics-bridge codebase, where they produced roughly 28 false positives against a hand-checked list of 20.) Omitted: 0 module(s) under scripts/. Their public functions are CLI commands registered by decorator, invisible to a uses-graph, so every one of them would appear here on every run. Vulture covers them in the dead-code section instead, where decorator awareness is built in.

Private names used across module boundaries

Cross-reference: Check 1. One row per module that reaches into a private name defined somewhere else. Keyed by the module doing the reaching, because that is the file that has to change.
column meaning
module the module doing the reaching, common prefix stripped
attr SLF001 — attribute access, other._private(...)
import PLC2701 — from other import _private
total the two summed; the tracker follows this as a proxy metric over time
names the private names touched, de-duplicated
Generated by: 
ruff check src tests \
    --select SLF001,PLC2701 --preview --output-format json
--preview is not optional: PLC2701 is preview-gated, and without the flag Ruff prints "Selection PLC2701 has no effect" and reports none of them. The project's own Ruff configuration still applies, so a per-file-ignores entry excusing these rules is respected — the count measures what policy does not already excuse. import is the column that matters. Importing a private module (_common, _logging) is idiomatic; importing a private function is coupling to an implementation detail. And a private function whose only outside caller is its own test is how a carpet survives: it looks used to a coverage gate while nothing in the package needs it. White-box testing is legitimate, so a high attr count over the test tree is not by itself a defect. Read this table for movement, not for a target of zero.
module attr import total names

Intra-module call depth

Cross-reference: Check 4. One row per src module whose own functions call each other at least 3 levels deep. Within one module, public functions should sit at one level of abstraction and privates one below, so a long chain means the module holds a ladder.
column meaning
module dotted module path, common prefix stripped
depth edges in the longest call chain among that module's own callables
cc1 of the functions in the chain, how many radon scores at complexity 1
chain the chain itself, caller first
Generated by: 
pyan3 src tests --root . --uses --no-defines --dot
radon cc src -j
pyan3 supplies the edges and radon the cc1 count; networkx computes the longest path after condensing cycles, so mutual recursion counts once instead of running forever. Where several chains tie at the longest length the lexicographically smallest is shown, so the row does not change between runs. cc1 is the discriminator, not depth. A deep chain of complexity-1 functions is a carpet — each layer only forwards to the next. A deep chain of substantial functions is usually a structural descent, and correct.

Folder cohesion

Do the folders correspond to clusters in the import graph — more dependencies within a folder than between folders? Like every number in the carpet report, these flag a boundary for triage and never adjudicate one. Do not move a module to improve a ratio. Scope: carpet_scan, 10 modules and 20 import edges between them.

Cohesion per folder

Cross-reference: Check 6. One row per folder: of every import edge with at least one end inside it, the share that stays inside. Direction is deliberately ignored — a folder everything imports and a folder that imports everything are equally uncohesive, and which end initiated is a question for the layering gate, not this table.
column meaning
folder package path, common prefix stripped
modules modules that are files; package nodes are excluded
internal edges with both ends in this folder
external edges with exactly one end in it, either direction
cohesion internal / (internal + external)
Generated by: 
python -c "import grimp; grimp.build_graph('carpet_scan')"
A folder holding fewer than 2 modules cannot have an internal edge at all, so its ratio is reported as n/a rather than 0%. Low cohesion is not automatically a defect. An orchestration folder — CLI entry points, workflows, adapters — earns its keep precisely by importing across the tree, and will measure near zero however well it is written. Read this table for folders that were meant to be cohesive units and are not.
folder modules internal external cohesion
<root> 10 20 0 100%

The clusters the graph actually has

Community detection partitions the same graph without being shown the folder names, so the result is what the imports say the modules are, independent of where they were filed. Comparing the two partitions is the measurement:
partition modularity Q
the folders you declared 0.000
the graph's own best split (2 communities) 0.139
20/20 edges (100%) stay inside a folder. A gap between the two Q values is a finding to triage, not a defect. Modularity rewards clustered topologies. A deliberately layered design cuts across features by construction — every feature contributes a module to the adapter layer, one to the workflow layer, and so on — so its folder partition will always score below a clustering found by maximising modularity, no matter how disciplined the layering is. What the gap tells you is that folder membership and coupling are answering different questions; whether that is intended is a judgement the numbers cannot make. What is worth acting on is a folder appearing in several clusters while its clusters each have an obvious name — that is one folder holding two unrelated things, and the split below says where the seam runs. Generated by: 
python -c "import grimp; grimp.build_graph('carpet_scan')"
python -c "import networkx; networkx.community.louvain_communities(g, seed=0)"
The community search is seeded (seed=0) so unchanged code produces an identical report; like the carpet report, this file carries no timestamp and is meant to be diffed between runs.
